title: How autism diagnoses can harm disabled children
author: Educating Hatbeasts
summary: Writing as the parent of two autistic boys, the author argues that the autism label often hides more useful information about a child's disabilities. Starting from an incident at an event for neurodivergent children, where a girl with a rare genetic disorder and severe working memory disability looked typical, she introduces the idea of Submarine Children whose real needs sit below the surface. She says the problem is not overdiagnosis but that complex children collect a laundry list of diagnoses and everyone, including clinicians and schools, fixates on autism even when it is not the most useful one. Her elephant in a pink fedora metaphor and De Bono's distinction between a bundle idea and a named idea explain how the label shuts down curiosity. She cites her younger son, whose school gave him the standard autism package while neglecting his sensory-motor disabilities, and concludes that autism should be the start of an investigation, not the end of it.
points: Many disabled children are 'Submarine Children' who look typical, so visible behaviour is a poor guide to the true extent of their needs.
The harm is not overdiagnosis but diagnostic fixation: autism becomes the headline label and crowds out more useful explanations.
A named idea like autism can limit understanding, and the article uses it to explain why clinicians dismiss regressions and neurological conditions as just more autism.
Schools that apply a standardised autism package can miss specific disabilities such as sensory-motor difficulties that actually drive a child's day.
Treat a diagnosis as the beginning of an investigation, and describe children through the specific functional issues that help adults respond.
quotes: Over time, I’ve started thinking of kids like Handstand Girl and Smaller Boy as ‘Submarine Children’. That is, kids who can appear typically developing to a casual onlooker, but turn out not to be.

People expect disability to be immediately visible - the child who struggles to walk, who can’t speak, or whose tics constantly jerk their entire body. Ideally, for easy recognition, the child should visibly struggle with all of those things simultaneously. When they do, their level of disability is assumed to be in direct proportion to the degree to which their behaviour disturbs the calm waters of neurotypicality.

Treatments for autism, such as ABA, traditionally focused on extinguishing visible signs of autism, such as stimming. The assumption was, if the child doesn’t look disabled, they’ll be more socially accepted (rather than realising the stims were simply an outward sign of something more serious).

The difficulty here isn’t kids being ‘overdiagnosed’ because they don’t meet the diagnostic criteria. They’re not non-disabled or mentally ill, either. The problem is an ‘autism’ diagnosis can be, in practice, like finding an elephant wearing a small pink fedora in your living room. I mean, sure, the elephant is legitimately wearing the hat, no question about it, but millinery is somewhat irrelevant to the literal elephant being there.

She argues, correctly, ‘autism’ is too often used to shutdown clinicians’ curiosity. I’ve learned severe regressions, chiari malformation and repeat ear infections , and even catatonia have wound up dismissed as ‘just more autism
Smaller Boy’s school also neglected his sensory-motor disabilities because they were too focused on giving him the standardised ‘autism package

And I think that’s a fundamental problem with ‘autism’. The problem here isn’t who is being diagnosed or not, whether they’re ‘really' disabled, if there are too many of them, or whether it’s now being treated as an identity rather than a disability. The problem is that kids with complex neurodevelopmental and neurological issues tend to attract a laundry list of diagnoses and descriptors and, out of those, everyone seems to focus in on ‘autism’ - even when it’s not the most useful or important one.

I only know both my children have sensory processing disabilities, with Smaller Boy’s significantly affecting his balance and movement, because ‘autism’ was simply the start of my investigations - not the end of them.
